segments.enText: (“OK, I do davening, but I don’t enjoy it!”)

OK, I get that. That is actually the most common comment made by young people who struggle with davening. “Did you daven this morning?” “No.” “Why not?” “I dunno.” “I dunno is not an answer!” “I dunno — I just don’t DO davening.”

So we need to figure out why you don’t do davening, or even if you do daven, why you find it so hard and not enjoyable. You’ve heard all the mussar shmoozes, speeches, guest speakers, Yom Iyuns, workshops, and Biur Tefillah classes. You’ve read all the books, tried all the workbooks, workshops, methods, and surefire tricks. You’ve been offered prizes — and threatened. Yet, for some reason, you look at the siddur and freeze! Or worse — you open it, try your hardest to daven, and mess up! Then you feel even more guilty than you did before, and you’re more convinced than ever that “Hashem certainly will not answer a mess-up like me!” Now you’re even further from your goal! And you do want to daven and enjoy davening (or at least you want to want to daven and enjoy it). You see that bachur shokeling away with his face contorted with emotion, or that girl with her siddur stuck right up to her face crying, and you wonder, “Why can’t I be like them? What’s the matter with me?”

But maybe that’s the problem! Perhaps you’re trying to be them. Perhaps you’re trying to be someone else. That’s not how tefillah works! ואני תפילתי—my tefillah is a reflection of the real “me.” As we explain in this siddur, first we proclaim, “זה א-לי ואנוהו—This is my G-d (I will create my own personal relationship with Hashem),” and then we say, “אלוקי אבי וארממנהו—He is the G-d of my father (and that unique relationship will be built on the foundations of our ancestors).” You need to be yourself — and being yourself can be quite scary and difficult. If you can’t learn to have a sincere conversation with yourself, then you’ll certainly find it difficult to talk to Hashem! So maybe it’s not the siddur; maybe it’s you! But the more you learn to be open with yourself, the easier it will be to talk to Hashem! And while this won’t always be easy, recognizing the issue is half the battle. And now you have something to ask Hashem: “Please, Hashem, help me become accepting of myself, able to see my potential, to recognize what I need to improve, and to have the courage to ask for help to become the best me possible!” That is certainly a good starting point!

Perhaps there are other possible reasons you “don’t do davening.” Perhaps you have questions — Hashem doesn’t seem fair, He never answers anyway, etc. OK — the FAQs section in this book addresses those questions. Perhaps you don’t understand the Hebrew? OK — there are translations. Perhaps you don’t understand the English? OK — so use this siddur; it’s easy to understand! Perhaps you’re afraid that if you actually daven, it will make the adults in your life happy, which will cause them to start demanding more of you (like when you suddenly get an 80 instead of your usual 65 and they respond: “Great! If you can get an 80, then next time you can get a 90!”). Or maybe — even worse — you’re afraid of your reputation! You’ve created this persona of a “non-davener” and you’re comfortable with that since it is safe and doesn’t demand much from you (you can’t mess up being a non-davener!). If you start davening, what will the chevrah say? What will all your BFFs say?

OK — I hear that. So don’t “daven” then. Talk to Hashem. When? On your way to yeshiva or school. In English. No siddur required — just have a conversation with Him about your life, what’s going on, and where you could use some help. (You won’t even look weird — people will assume you have a Bluetooth!)

I once walked into my ninth-grade Chumash class when I was giving a test. I saw a girl mumbling to herself and assumed that she was reviewing Rashi. When I got closer, I heard she was saying, “Please, Hashem, let Mashiach come before Rabbi Feigenbaum gives this test!” I told her that it looked like that wasn’t going to happen. When her face fell, I suggested she ask Hashem that Mashiach should come before I grade her test! Her face lit up and she blurted out, “Oy, Hashem, please let Mashiach come before Rabbi Feigenbaum grades this test!” That was a 100 percent true, heartfelt conversation with Hashem. (Unfortunately for her and for all of us, what she wanted didn’t happen. So why did Hashem turn down her request? See the FAQs.)

But I would like to suggest one last possible reason why it is hard for you to daven. Davening is a middah, like patience, generosity, social skills, or organization. Hashem creates people different. Everyone has stuff that is naturally difficult for them, and they must work really hard to get it right. Take me: I have poor math skills, sloppy handwriting, and I struggle with knowing when to stop talking and start listening. Everybody has things that are easier for them and things that are harder: Some boys have zitzfleish and can sit for hours concentrating on a sugya. Others lose their place after a few seconds — even though they can fix every broken desk in five minutes! Some girls by their nature love going to visit old ladies in old age homes. They find it fun — “Oh, they’re so cute” — and naturally do that chessed. Others find it painful: Old age homes make them nervous, they don’t know what to say, and they feel like dorks. The same is true with davening. Some people, by their G-d-given nature, enjoy davening. They were born with good language skills, and the words speak to them — it’s just their thing! For others, it’s simply a battle. Just like some kids always seem to know what to say and the chevrah are always crowding around them, and others find themselves constantly in awkward social situations. Or for some girls, tz’niyus comes naturally, and for others it’s a struggle. That’s how Hashem created us; we each have our own strengths, weaknesses, likes, dislikes, and battles.

It is self-understood that Hashem expects you to do the best you can — not less. But He also doesn’t expect you to be someone else! So what to do? I can’t help you with your school rules or your parents’ expectations. Forget those for a moment. More important is your relationship with Hashem. It’s a slow process. That’s OK. Start slow. How about one Asher Yatzar in the morning. Read it slowly and really think about how lucky you are that you can go to the bathroom and say thank you — in English! Take one brachah of the Shemoneh Esrei each week and stop, read the English explanation, and think about what it means to you — and tell Hashem what you’re thinking.
One brachah! All growth is in stages.

Be wary of what the mussar sefarim call the “frum yetzer hara.” He gets you to jump too fast, too far, too quick. Then you fall and thus convince yourself that you’re a loser — and give up! They say that Rav Shach, zt”l, on Rosh Hashanah accepted upon himself that once a day he would be careful to say bentching from a siddur rather than by heart. And he didn’t promise himself to do this forever but until Chanukah! Something doable so you feel you accomplished something. Then on to the next step.

Will this be a steady climb up? Nope! Not at all! You’ll have bad days and crash. We all do. (Remember, an EKG that’s a straight and smooth line means you are dead!) I too have found myself walking backward and saying, “Oh, I guess I just finished Shemoneh Esrei” — and I wrote this siddur!

The Satmar Rebbe, zy”a, used to say the following: “Eileh va’rechev v’eileh va’susim” — when the non-Jew wants to travel, he needs horses and chariots. But “anachnu b’sheim Hashem Elokeinu nazkir” — if we want to “travel,” all we need to do is start davening and our minds are all over the place!
So don’t be afraid to join the club of those who struggle every day to focus, think seriously, and actually have a heart-to-heart talk with our Creator.

How will this siddur help? This is not a full and literal translation of all the tefillos. Rather, it is an overview of what I believe to be the basic main point of each part of the weekday siddur, written in simple English in order to help you talk to Hashem. In addition, it deals with the common questions we all have when we take our davening and relationship with Hashem seriously.

Of course, whenever possible, you should say the tefillos in the original Hebrew and use this merely as an aid in understanding what you are saying. Chazal have infused our tefillos with many very special meanings. There’s a reason why it’s called Lashon Hakodesh! But remember, Hashem understands all languages as long as the person speaking is sincere and honest! (BTW, throughout this siddur I use Hebrew words written in Ashkenazic transliteration, and generally did not translate them in order not to mess up the flow. But there is an extensive glossary in the back — don’t be shy to use it!)

Of all the “Instant Insights” in this siddur, the following is my favorite, on the pasuk in Ashrei: “קרוב ה׳ לכל קוראיו—Hashem is close to all who call to Him”; “לכל אשר יקראהו באמת—but one must call out to Hashem with אמת—honesty and sincerity.” It doesn’t say that Hashem is close to all “קראהו באמת,” who now call to Him with honesty and integrity. Rather, “אשר יקראהו באמת—who will call (in the future tense) to Him with honesty.” This means that if right now you have a very up-and-down relationship with Hashem, you struggle with being 100 percent sincere 100 percent of the time, and at times you’re a bit of a hypocrite as far as what you promise Hashem and what you end up doing — still, as long as you are committed to being “יקראהו באמת,” i.e., your goal is to be completely sincere, honest, and genuine in your relationship with Hashem, then already now He will listen to Your requests for help to get there!

If used properly, honestly, and diligently, this siddur will help you take your tefillah to a higher level, help you get back up when you’ve had “one of those days,” and give you the tools to be the best davener you can be. And that is all Hashem asks of us.

First of all, this is not a literal translation. Nor does it explain every word or sentence of every tefillah. Many tefillos have multiple layers of meaning, and at times, a literal translation makes certain sentences appear repetitious when we know that in reality, they are not. My goal was to be brief, convey what I understand to be the essence of the tefillah, and facilitate a meaningful conversation with Hashem.

Thus at times, long paragraphs have only a few lines of English (e.g., Hodu and Az Yashir). In addition, you may find it difficult to see where what I have said is found in the specific words of a tefillah (especially Tehillim). That is because the mefarshim and midrashim I used to explain that tefillah add ideas based on the context of that chapter within the Sefer Tehillim, and within the context of David HaMelech’s life.

Tefillos that I felt are most central and are rarely skipped (e.g., Ashrei) I explained in greater detail and I tried to stick closer to the actual words. But even in such instances, I added words into the translation in order to make it more personal, readable, or convey the essence of the meaning as understood by the mefarshim. To denote that these words are not found in the text itself, they will be in italics: e.g., “אַשְׁרֵי יוֹשְׁבֵי בֵיתֶךָ—Happy are those who (wherever they are) are living in the house of Hashem.” That addition in italics is based on the commentary of Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, who explains that with the proper values and mindset, any home, wherever it is, can become “the house of Hashem” even if it is not situated in Yerushalayim or the Beis Hamikdash.

In addition, commentaries like the Malbim and Rav Hirsch stress time and time again that many words in Lashon Hakodesh have multiple meanings, but those meanings are all interconnected if one understands the depth behind them. My choice of translation of certain key words was based on what I felt fit the meaning in that context, using terms that teens could relate to, and would most create a sense of real conversation and connection with Hashem. A few examples of translations that do not fit the norm:
• ברוך as in ברוך אתה ה׳—You, Hashem, are the Source of everything, as explained by Derech Hachaim quoting the Avudraham, Rabbi Munk, and others.
• קדוש as in אתה קדוש—You, Hashem, are separate and removed from this physical world, as Rashi explains קדושה at the beginning of Parashas Kedoshim.

• שם as in ישתבח שמך or ברוך שם—May the impact of all You do (שמך) be praised; or May the perception of Hashem’s Presence be increased, as in the pasuk: “טוב שם משמן טוב—A good reputation is better than good oil” (Koheles 7:1). שם refers to reputation or how someone is known.

Throughout this siddur I have used Hebrew words, terms, and concepts written in Ashkenazic transliteration. In order not to impede the flow, I chose in general not to translate them, but I have provided an extensive glossary at the end of the siddur so that this work will be accessible to all.

pieces.title: Introduction for Parents, Mechanchim, and Mechanchos

segments.enText: It was Friday morning at a Torah Umesorah convention. Principals of girls’ high schools were sitting around a table (a “networking” breakfast, for those familiar), and someone posed a question: “We’re having such a problem with davening in school! Does anyone have any ideas?” And someone responded, “Is there anyone who is not having a problem with the davening in school?”

Tefillah is the Achilles’ heel of chinuch — both in school and at home. One can mandate putting on tefillin, and whether the boy is engaged with the mitzvah or not, he has nonetheless put on tefillin! If a girl’s skirt is appropriate, she is tzanua whether she is wearing it that way out of love for the sanctity of tz’niyus or because she doesn’t want to get a detention! But mumbling Hebrew words in order to avoid dirty looks from the “prison warden” who is wandering up and down the aisles glaring at people (or from your father sitting next to you) — that’s not tefillah! It may look like a beautiful davening to the outsider watching, and you can boast, “See, our students/my children don’t talk during davening!” But in reality, all it accomplishes is the creation of PTSD (post-traumatic siddur disorder). When that young person sees a siddur later in life, or walks into a shul as an adult, they’ll have flashbacks and feel anxiety and pain.

Tefillah is “avodah she’ba’lev,” and it is meant to be a very personal and heartfelt communication with Hashem. The siddur is supposed to help facilitate that connection. Chazal wove many deep, meaningful, and lofty ideas and concepts into the tefillos. Much of tefillah is Tehillim, which are certainly meant to convey many layers of beauty and meaning. Unfortunately, in today’s world, many young people (and adults) are not comfortable with Lashon Hakodesh, and even the English translations do not always “speak” to them; besides the fact that many phrases defy translation. In addition, teenagers (and adults — but we try not to let teens know that) have many complex and sticky questions about the tefillos and about their day-to-day relationship with Hashem. These questions get stuck in their brain and impede their ability to talk to Hashem honestly and openly.

So how will this siddur help? This is not a full and literal translation of all the tefillos. Rather, it is an overview of what I believe to be the basic main point of each part of the weekday siddur, written in simple English, using terms that are relevant to today’s teenagers. The translations, explanations, and concepts were culled from a wide variety of sources (mefarshei haTanach, mefarshei tefillah, sifrei mussar, hashkafah, and chassidus), mixing, matching, and merging — even within the same pasuk — in order to create a work that is hashkafically sound, meaningful, and readable. In addition, it deals with the common questions we all have when we take our davening and relationship with Hashem seriously. My goal is to ease the “angst” of these questions, while helping teens (and us!) understand something of what the tefillos are meant to convey, thereby making it easier for all of us to pour out our hearts to Hashem on a daily basis.

Will this solve all tefillah problems? Nope! After spending months studying the tefillos and writing this commentary, I still find myself at times taking three steps backward and saying to myself, “Oh! I guess I just finished Shemoneh Esrei!” (Sound familiar?) For some people, because of their G-d-given nature, davening will always be easy (just like for some people, because of their nature, they will have an easier time being patient or charitable). And for some, because of their G-d-given nature, davening will be hard (just like for some people, because of their nature, they will have a harder time being patient or charitable). We all have areas of avodas Hashem that are easier or harder. But if used properly, in conjunction with a positive atmosphere and healthy chinuch, this siddur will help your children and students be the best daveners they can be. And you will learn much in the process!

pieces.title: A Personal Note from Rabbi Feigenbaum

segments.enText: For Parents, Mechanchim, and Mechanchos
“Are you sure my kid/student should be reading this? I grew up fine without all this stuff!”

Me too! I went to school in the ’50s and ’60s, and I don’t remember asking any of these questions! In addition, as you are well aware, today there are a plethora of books on the overall topic of emunah — how to approach it, if to approach it, intellectual analysis, appeals to the emotions, self-awareness, new-age and old-age, and so on! In addition, there are many books and sefarim that deal with very specific issues of Torah hashkafah, and many of these works are heavily footnoted, showing a level of erudition of Rishonim and Acharonim that surpasses my knowledge base. So what are this siddur and appendix doing?

I am basing myself on my unique area of expertise — the frum teenager. In order to pasken any issue properly, one needs to be an expert in the reality of the issue. And as far as the reality of teenagers goes, I have merited over the past forty years to have many DMCs (deep and meaningful conversations) with your mainstream “good” frum yeshiva bachurim/Bais Yaakov girls from all over North America, England, and Israel. Many of these DMCs have been in person and many have been by email. And I’m not talking about those who might be termed “messed-up” or “off-the-derech” hanging out on street corners. Those kids are doing fine! They are being honest with where they are holding, and we have invested financial and human resources to create programs to educate them, validate them, embrace them, and thus get them back. I am talking instead about the “good” kids — the “don’t ask, don’t tell,” or the “walk the walk, talk the talk” kids. Those are the ones who are either acting out somewhat (or a lot), but under the radar, or who are not acting out but are simply unexcited — either way, they are full of questions. In every community, in every “style” of education, no matter how sheltered and heimishe or large and metropolitan, no matter “in town” or “out of town” — they are all the same! They’re all asking the same questions and all share the same nagging concerns. And that is fine!

As Harav Wolbe, zt”l, would say, “There is no such thing as an apikorsus question — only apikorsus answers.” The only difference is that the good kids are street-smart enough to keep those questions to themselves in order not to become a “case.”

Harav Aharon Feldman, shlita, Rosh Yeshivas Ner Israel of Baltimore, summed it up very succinctly at a Torah Umesorah convention when he said, “We are raising a generation of young people who are very observant, but not very religious.”

The opening essay (“But I Don’t Do Davening”) and the following answers to the questions were written for teens — not adults! Adults are working with different assumptions, have a very different knowledge base, have different life experiences (for better or for worse), and adults and teens use different words to mean different things (we do not speak the same language!). Simply put, adults and teens read things with different glasses. If the following makes sense to you and helps, great! If not, then get one of the many books written for adults. And if this will generate more questions in your son or daughter or students — then ashreichem! You will have a wonderful opportunity to fulfill “v’shinantam l’vanecha” in a meaningful way!
Much hatzlachah!
For Teens

I assume you read the introduction for the adults! Before getting to the answers, I want to make three very important points about questions. As I said above, questions are fine. As Harav Wolbe, zt”l, would say, “There is no such thing as an apikorsus question — only apikorsus answers.” But (there always is a “but”) …

1. As much as we all wish our daily experience of Torah and mitzvos to be understandable, uplifting, meaningful, and exciting, the truth is that for most people, at times in our lives, it is not! Still, the bedrock of our emunah is that Hashem spoke at Har Sinai and chose us for a mission (which is borne out by our miraculous existence until today, which makes no sense — much to the consternation of the rest of the world!), and therefore, simply put, we must get with the program and do the best we can! And that is the first brachah of our daily Birchos HaTorah, which is specifically “la’asok b’divrei Sorah” — you just have to do it! You have questions? Fine. Good! Understanding and connecting more is great. The second brachah is “v’haarev na” — that Torah should be sweet and understandable; that is our goal! However, it can take years and years to ask all the questions and get the answers. Until that happens, we must start with la’asok — to get with the program and just do it as well as we can. As we said inside the siddur: “Seichel tov” — A good understanding of Torah is given, “l’chol oseihem” — to those who practice it! So you should certainly ask questions, but keep “doing Torah” while you figure things out.

2. Your questions must be honest questions and not excuses. Meaning, you need to be honest with yourself. Are you involved in inappropriate stuff and you need an excuse so that you don’t feel guilty? (“Hey, it’s OK to do x, y, z because this stuff doesn’t make sense anyways!”) Is that why you are asking your questions? If that is your motivation, then don’t waste your time. People who do that read this section with the goal of not liking the answers in order to say to themselves, “See, I read the book, I’m still not convinced, so now I can go and mess up my life.” I once spoke to a young lady who told me, “I’m working on making sure that Yiddishkeit is not true, because if it is, I am doomed to a life of gloom and doom!” I felt bad that her experience of Torah and mitzvos was so negative, but she wasn’t asking questions, so I couldn’t give her answers! So try to be honest and aim high. If you’re like most teens I’ve met — honest, growing, sincere young people with neshamos thirsting for some clarity — then hopefully this will help a bit.

3. These are all complex topics. Entire books have been written on each of these questions. My goal here is to give some basic sense of how to approach these topics and give enough clarity that these questions will not get in the way of your davening. But there is much more to these topics than what is written here. If these answers raise even more questions, great! Go find books on the subject, ask your rebbeim and morahs, or email me at rabbiyfeigenbaum@gmail.com, and I will try to clarify things.
Thanks for listening, and may you have much success in your growth to becoming a quality, contributing, and confident ben Torah/bas Yisrael.
In loving memory of

segments.heText: גליקל חנה בת חיים וחיה צינה ע”ה

segments.enText: **Mrs. Gloria Cohen ע”ה**
Thornhill, Canada
The oldest child of survivors of the Shoah, her parents emigrated to Canada to begin life anew, while retaining the Torah values of their upbringing.
Named after two grandmothers, she was a bridge to the Torah and Yiddishkeit that infused the shtetls of Staszow and Kusnica, where most of the Jewish residents perished al Kiddush Hashem.
Family, Torah and tefillah were her life, and a siddur and Tehillim were never far from her hands.
She led her life with those eternal principles in mind and made those values the pillars of her house.

With a kind disposition and a compassionate demeanor, she was a friend to many, a cherished member of her community, a devoted wife to her husband, a loving Eema and Bubby to her children and grandchildren, and is dearly missed by all.
In loving memory of

segments.heText: שרה טעלצא בת יבדלחט”א לוי שמחה גאלדמאן

segments.enText: **Sara Goldman ע”ה**
A teenager who understood the power of tefillah, was constantly searching for ever-deeper meaning, and was of exemplary middos to all those around her
Li’chvod my Rosh Yeshiva
**HaRav Yitzchak Feigenbaum**

You have always been an inspiration to me. You personify what a true Torah Jew is and have shown me by example a love for learning. I miss your Thursday night shmuzim and still hear your niggunim for the Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur davening in my head every year. I wish you much mazal and brachah on the completion of this siddur. May Hashem bless you, your rebbetzin, and your entire family with good health and happiness until 120.
With much love and gratitude,
**AVI AND ILANA TOBIAS**
**Mr. Mayer Rosenzweig**
**Mr. Josh Salmon**
If ever there were a situation where one should start their acknowledgments by thanking Hashem, it is surely when writing a commentary on a siddur!

Yet, to be honest, I struggle with that. Whenever I see authors start by offering thanks to Hashem, I’ve always thought to myself, “Duh! Isn’t that obvious? Does it really need to be said?” But I now understand that it does need to be said! (See FAQs for why.) But more importantly, I learned what I am thanking Him for. At the end of Modim D’Rabbanan, there is a curious phrase, “Al she’anachnu modim lach,” and I struggled to understand what it meant. I discovered that we are thanking Hashem “for instilling in us the concept and (crucial) character trait of gratitude!” It’s so easy (at least for some of us) to confidently roll along feeling that we’re in control — just that we need Hashem to not “get in our way.” What a tragic mistake. As I look back at all the details Hashem had to put into place in order to get me to the point of putting out this siddur, it is humbling indeed! So I do want to offer shevach v’hodaah l’Hashem Yisbarach, but not simply for giving me the wherewithal to produce this work. More importantly, I want to thank Him for giving me the ability to recognize His Hand in all areas of my life, being able to recognize my strengths and know my limitations, and most importantly, for having sense enough to thank Him for all that!

Clearly, without the support, understanding, and binah yeseirah of my eishes chayil, Chaya Lana, my chinuch career would never have happened. So many times, I was simply MIA at crucial moments, yet she kept the ship afloat and allowed me to help others. And from experience I have learned how true it is that our wives are blessed with a binah yeseirah. Her insights and intuition have proven invaluable time and time again. She truly knows me better than I know myself and has helped me keep my balance. Of course, my entire family, kids, kids-in-law, grandkids, and great-grandkids have been a huge support in so many ways. And they were always there for that important constructive criticism that only close family can offer. My daughter Batya deserves a special shout-out; her addition to our family had a profound effect in so many ways! But regarding this siddur, it is truly her brainchild. It was her idea, she constantly pushed me forward, and she was my in-house expert on all things “teenager.” In the merit of all the tefillos generated by this siddur, may Hashem answer all her requests.

“U’mi’talmidai yoser mi’kulam.” Over the last forty-five years, I have been blessed with amazing talmidim and talmidos who have constantly inspired me with their honesty and spurred me to new levels of understanding by their questions. To all of you I can truly say, “She’eilas chacham chatzi teshuvah”; your honesty forced me to be honest! Over the last eighteen years, my talmidos in Tiferes Bais Yaakov have allowed me to try out explanations, concepts, and sources and have enabled me to develop the approach to chinuch and the hashkafah curriculum that is reflected in this siddur. To all of them, and to all those who took care of the material needs of Tiferes so that I had a free hand to develop the ruchniyus, what more can I say but … thank you!

“Acharon acharon chaviv.” In life, it doesn’t matter what you say, but rather, what people thought you said! And in chinuch that is most certainly true! In addition, what we hear is affected by what we see! From simply taking care of my poor grammar (we didn’t do grammar in the ’60s!) to taking complex ideas and ensuring people would “hear” what I “said,” the staff at Mosaica Press have used their extensive, G-d-given skills in a most marvelous way! And then they took all that and turned it into a user-friendly siddur that is a paradigm of “zeh Keili v’anveihu.” But I’m not surprised. From my first meeting with Rabbi Haber and Rabbi Kornbluth, it was clear that they “got it” (the highest compliment in “teenage-ese”). They understood the need, they had vision, and they are people devoted to helping educate Klal Yisrael. Once I realized that, it was obvious that the best thing I could do was to leave this siddur in their good hands. And the results speak for themselves. Special mention must be made of Mrs. Gross and Mrs. Broyde. Even more than their expertise (and their considerable patience with me), it was their vision and dedication that made every page of this siddur a literary and aesthetic work of art.

To all those who had a hand in taking this siddur from an abstract concept to its present form, I bentch you with what we say three times daily in Shema Koleinu: “U’mi’lefanecha malkeinu reikam al teshiveinu — Do not turn us away empty-handed.” In this siddur we gave the following explanation: Of course, we hope that Hashem will grant us what we have requested. But sometimes, for reasons known only to Him, Hashem must say no. We therefore ask Hashem that if the answer to our tefillah must be no, then at least He should not send us away feeling “empty-handed,” i.e., with a feeling of total rejection. Let our hearts always be filled with emunah that we had the amazing zechus and opportunity to talk one-on-one with Hashem and that He heard our tefillah — even if the best thing for us right now is a no.
